Context/Background: Perianal fistulizing Crohn’s disease (CD) is a severe gastrointestinal disorder causing extensive mucosal damage with limited treatment options. Severe manifestations of the disease appear at higher rates in non-Europeans but the genetic and cellular mechanisms driving the disease phenotypes remain poorly understood. Herein, we tested whether pathologic determinants in the epithelial stem cell compartment could be detected at the transcript level in rectal organoids derived from a diverse patient population. Rectal organoid and mucosal cells from endoscopic biopsies of each patient having perianal fistulizing CD or no disease controls were prepared for and sequenced at the single cell level. After cell type annotations based on expressed marker genes, samples were analyzed by principal components, for differential transcript expression, cell type proportions, and pathway enrichment.
Prompt: To assess differences in pathway activity based on transcription profiles between the mucosa epithelial cells and the corresponding patient derived organoids, we calculated pathway enrichment scores for paired Mucosa vs Organoids.  Please give a summary of the pathway enrichment results.  Focus on highlighting similarities and differences in the UP (Mucosa enriched) and DOWN (Organoid enriched) pathways.
output_text:
Introduction/Context  
The provided table (“Supplemental Table 3”) lists Reactome pathways significantly enriched in mucosal epithelial cells (UP) versus patient‐derived rectal organoids (DOWN) from paired biopsies in perianal fistulizing Crohn’s disease.  Directionality refers to higher transcript enrichment in mucosa (UP) or in organoids (DOWN).  Sample sizes, sequencing depth, cell‐type breakdowns, and exact p-values are not specified in the table.

Keywords  
• vesicle-mediated transport  
• cell cycle checkpoints  
• Rho GTPase signaling  
• RNA metabolism  
• stress response  

Candidate Genes  
• CFTR  
• SERPINA1  
• RAB27A  
• ATM  
• ATR  
• CDK1  

Pathway Enrichments  

Up (Mucosa-enriched) Pathways (top by gene count)  
| Theme                                                   | Direction | GeneCount |
|---------------------------------------------------------|-----------|-----------|
| VESICLE-MEDIATED TRANSPORT                              | UP        | 224       |
| MEMBRANE TRAFFICKING                                    | UP        | 222       |
| SIGNALING BY RHO GTPASES                                | UP        | 207       |
| METABOLISM OF RNA                                       | UP        | 193       |
| CELLULAR RESPONSES TO STIMULI                           | UP        | 192       |
| CELLULAR RESPONSES TO STRESS                            | UP        | 185       |
| METABOLISM OF LIPIDS                                    | UP        | 174       |
| CHROMATIN ORGANIZATION                                  | UP        | 92        |
| ANTIGEN PROCESSING: UBIQUITINATION & PROTEASOME DEGRAD. | UP        | 84        |

Down (Organoid-enriched) Pathways (top by gene count)  
| Theme                        | Direction | GeneCount |
|------------------------------|-----------|-----------|
| CELL CYCLE CHECKPOINTS       | DOWN      | 93        |
| DNA REPAIR                   | DOWN      | 90        |
| MTORC1-MEDIATED SIGNALLING   | DOWN      | 9         |
| CONDENSATION OF PROMETAPHASE | DOWN      | 9         |
| G2/M TRANSITION EVENTS       | DOWN      | 9         |
| DOWNREGULATION OF TGF-β SIG. | DOWN      | 9         |
| HSFI ACTIVATION              | DOWN      | 9         |
| LEADING STRAND SYNTHESIS     | DOWN      | 9         |
| mRNA DECAY                   | DOWN      | 9         |
| AZATHIOPRINE ADME            | DOWN      | 9         |

Analysis  
1. Balance: Mucosa shows strong enrichment in >10 trafficking- and secretion-related modules (vesicle transport, Golgi trafficking, membrane remodeling) and in broad stress/immune response pathways (infectious disease, SARS-CoV-2, NFκB/STAT, cellular stress). Organoids are enriched largely for cell‐cycle and genome‐maintenance processes (cell cycle checkpoints, DNA repair, replication and condensin functions).  
2. Functional divergence: Epithelial mucosa retains in vivo functions—secretory traffic, lipid handling, environmental sensing and chromatin remodeling—supporting barrier and immune roles. Organoids prioritize proliferative homeostasis and DNA upkeep, consistent with an expanding stem/progenitor phenotype ex vivo.  
3. Shared themes: Both show Rho-GTPase signaling modules (cytoskeletal regulation) and core mRNA processing/chromatin organization, indicating common epithelial‐lineage programs preserved in culture.  
4. Clinical implication: The mucosa-driven stress and immune modules may underlie tissue pathology and interactions with microbiota, whereas enhanced cell-cycle and repair in organoids could reflect culture adaptation and may limit their direct modeling of epithelial damage in Crohn’s disease.  

Next Steps & Clarification  
1. Verify whether organoid upregulation of DNA repair correlates with proliferation markers (e.g., Ki67) via immunostaining.  
2. Assess functional vesicle trafficking differences by measuring secretion of key mucosal enzymes or cytokines in organoids vs. biopsies.  
3. Perform targeted inhibition of Rho-GTPase signaling to test effects on organoid morphology and barrier maturity.  
4. Determine whether prominent mucosa stress-response genes (e.g., HSPA5, NFE2L2) are driven by microbial cues by co-culture assays with commensal bacteria.
